strengths: Addresses an important limitation of RLVR: on very hard problems where the base model cannot sample a correct solution, reward gradients vanish; using expert human solutions is a sensible way to obtain learning signal without a stronger teacher.

The two-stage DAIL design is well motivated and technically interesting: a privileged student expands didactic expert solutions into more in-distribution traces, mixed policy rollouts preserve the student's natural reasoning while anchoring to the expert solution, and a contrastive objective with a negative reference penalizes rationalization shortcuts.

The empirical study is broad: two model families (Qwen2.5-Instruct and Qwen3-8B think), multiple math benchmarks (AIME 2024/2025, BeyondAIME, IMO-AnswerBench), an out-of-domain GPQA-Diamond evaluation, and baselines including direct SFT, STaR rationalization, temperature variation, GRPO, NuRL+GRPO, and GRPO on DeepScaleR.

The reported pass@k gains are substantial on several benchmarks, and the method uses fewer than 1000 expert solutions, supporting the claimed sample efficiency. The efficiency results under budget forcing also suggest real improvements in reasoning token usage.

Ablations/analyses support key design choices: contrastive loss outperforms NLL, mixed policy rollouts help Qwen3-8B (think), and DAIL's lower training-set fit coincides with better test generalization, consistent with the shortcut-learning motivation.
The paper releases a new Olympiad proof dataset (el-proof) sourced with permission and provides detailed prompts and training hyperparameters in the appendix, which is valuable for the community.
The offline formulation and LoRA-based memory sharing are practical advantages over online RLVR, and the paper reports compute costs that support the claimed training efficiency.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is limited: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests are reported despite small benchmarks (AIME 60, BeyondAIME 100, GPQA 198) and several small or mixed differences. The central 10-25% pass@k gains need uncertainty quantification, especially for OOD results where DAIL sometimes underperforms the base model (e.g., Qwen2.5 GPQA pass@128 85.9 vs 84.3; Qwen3 GPQA pass@1 at 4096 55.1 vs 54.7).

The central non-verifiable proof claim is not directly evaluated: the model is trained on Olympiad proofs (el-proof) but evaluated only on answer-verifiable math benchmarks and GPQA. There is no proof-generation or proof-validity evaluation, so the claim about learning on non-verifiable proof problems is only indirectly supported.

The contrastive loss equation is incomplete in the main text: only the positive KL term is fully shown, while the negative-reference term and the role of gamma are described verbally rather than written precisely. This hinders reproducibility and makes the exact objective hard to implement from the paper alone. There is also no formal stability analysis despite the potentially unbounded negative divergence term, only an empirical loss curve.

Mixed-policy rollout and truncation details are ambiguous. Appendix B.2 says reasoning-model rollouts are truncated at 256 tokens, but the main text implies full expanded reasoning traces. It is unclear how this affects long-CoT training and the claimed long-CoT reasoning improvements. The threshold tau is selected on training-set performance and fixed across models, with higher-correctness tau values rejected on qualitative grounds.

The negative reference is constructed by heuristic regular-expression extraction of numerical/symbolic waypoints. There is no analysis of extraction quality, coverage, or sensitivity, especially for proof and geometry problems. The contrastive objective may therefore penalize legitimate tokens along with shortcut-inducing ones, and the paper does not analyze which tokens are actually affected.

RLVR baseline comparisons have comparability concerns: el-verifiable consists of problems not solved in 32 base-model attempts, so standard GRPO may have extremely sparse or zero reward signal by construction. The paper acknowledges this but still uses the degradation as evidence against RLVR. NuRL+GRPO underperformance is attributed to hint reliance but is not fully isolated from implementation/tuning issues. It is also unclear whether baselines use the same LoRA/full fine-tuning setup and whether the A40-vs-H100 compute difference affects comparisons.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is mentioned, no random seeds or repeated runs are reported, and exact dataset release/license details are absent from the manuscript. Prompts and hyperparameters are provided, but the incomplete contrastive loss and ambiguous generation setup prevent reliable reimplementation.

The evaluation relies heavily on pass@k with large k (up to 128) while pass@1 is low, so practical greedy utility is limited. The token-efficiency claim is demonstrated via budget forcing but lacks exact per-budget numbers and statistical tests, making the 2x-4x efficiency claim harder to verify precisely.

Deduplication and leakage controls are only partially convincing: el-verifiable was not initially deduplicated against IMO-AnswerBench, and the post-hoc 15-problem overlap analysis is relegated to the appendix. The el-proof deduplication uses a heuristic SentenceBERT threshold of 0.7, with no sensitivity analysis.

Some claims are overbroad relative to the evidence, e.g., 'first demonstration' of improving long-CoT reasoning directly from expert solutions and 'enable out-of-domain generalization' despite small, mixed OOD gains. The limitations discussion is present but does not fully address the proof-evaluation gap or statistical uncertainty.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: learning from high-quality expert solutions when RLVR has zero reward and when problems are non-verifiable.
Proposes a plausible two-stage method (privileged-student generation plus contrastive learning) with an intuitive motivation about didactic vs. rationalization shortcuts.
For Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, includes a reasonably broad baseline set (SFT, STaR, temperature tuning, GRPO, NuRL, DeepScaleR) and ablations over loss, generation method, and hyperparameters.
Curates and promises to release a small expert Olympiad proof dataset (el-proof), which could be a useful resource.
Reports compute-efficiency analysis showing DAIL is much cheaper per epoch than online RLVR once synthetic traces are generated.
weaknesses: The core contrastive loss is not fully specified: the displayed equation is incomplete and omits the negative-reference term and gamma, making the central objective difficult to reproduce as written.

The central claim of enabling learning from non-verifiable proof problems is not directly evaluated. The paper trains on el-proof but evaluates only on verifiable answer benchmarks; it provides no proof-generation correctness, human evaluation, or other direct evidence of improved proof ability.

For the long-CoT LRM setting (Qwen3-8B think), the paper lacks key baselines such as direct SFT on expert solutions, STaR, or a comparable RLVR/hint baseline. The main LRM evidence is token-budget curves (likely pass@1) and GPQA, while abstract claims about pass@k gains on Qwen3 are not clearly supported in the main results.

No seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance are reported for pass@k on small benchmarks (e.g., 60 AIME problems). Differences of 1-2 points are likely within noise, so many claimed gains are not reliably established.

The negative-reference construction is ad hoc (regex-extracted waypoints) and is not validated as actually producing shortcut-laden reasoning. The contrastive objective is justified mainly by a training-set/test-set gap, which could have other explanations.

The mixed-policy rollout procedure and tau calibration are heuristic; tau is selected on the training set, and Qwen3 rollouts are truncated at 256 tokens, raising serious questions about whether the resulting traces can teach long-CoT reasoning.
Baseline comparisons may be unfair or under-tuned, especially SFT on expert solutions, GRPO/NuRL at small scale, and DeepScaleR with one epoch; compute-matched comparisons are missing.

The validation/hyperparameter-tuning protocol is ambiguous and potentially leaks information if the validation set is drawn from later AIME problems; even if not, it is a small in-domain validation set with no independent confirmation.

Claims are overstated relative to evidence: the abstract's '10-25% pass@k gains on Qwen2.5-Instruct and Qwen3 models' is not clearly demonstrated for Qwen3, out-of-domain GPQA gains are marginal with some drops, and 'first demonstration' claims are not well supported.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, the negative-reference regex is only partially specified, and the incomplete loss equation prevents exact reimplementation.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: learning from high-quality expert human solutions when standard RLVR fails due to the exploration/zero-reward bottleneck, especially for non-verifiable domains such as Olympiad proofs.

The DAIL method is well motivated and intuitively clear. The two-stage design—first expanding didactic expert solutions into in-distribution traces via a privileged student or mixed policy rollouts, then applying a contrastive objective to suppress rationalization shortcuts—directly targets the identified distribution mismatch.

Strong empirical evidence on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: consistent pass@k gains on AIME 2024/2025, BeyondAIME, and IMO-AnswerBench over base, direct SFT, STaR rationalization, GRPO, NuRL, and DeepScaleR+GRPO. The train-vs-test analysis in Figure 6 provides useful evidence that DAIL avoids shortcut imitation.
Useful ablations: contrastive loss vs NLL, mixed policy rollouts vs direct sampling for reasoning models, tau calibration, gamma selection, and loss-term ablations support the design choices.
Demonstrates practical benefits beyond accuracy: 2x–4x token efficiency under budget forcing and largely preserved or improved out-of-domain GPQA-Diamond performance.
Promising resource contribution: the curated el-proof dataset of 669 Olympiad proof problems with expert solutions, if actually released with clear licensing, would be valuable for the community.
Appendix provides substantial reproducibility detail: prompts, hyperparameters, LoRA settings, training compute, negative-reference construction, and data deduplication steps.
Research ethics and data provenance are handled reasonably: expert solutions were used with permission, and the impact statement is thoughtful.

Originality is solid: while related to rationalization, distillation, and speculative/interactive imitation, the specific combination of privileged-student expansion plus a negative-reference contrastive objective for expert-solution learning is novel and useful.
weaknesses: The abstract claims 10–25% pass@k gains on both Qwen2.5-Instruct and Qwen3, but the Qwen3 experiments in Figure 4 appear to report token-budget/pass@1-style performance rather than pass@k. No pass@k curves for Qwen3 are shown, so a central claim is not fully supported by the presented evidence.

The long-CoT/proof setting lacks key baselines. For Qwen3-8B (think) trained on el-proof, the paper compares only against the base model and direct vs mixed policy generation. There is no direct SFT on expert proofs or NLL-on-transformed-traces baseline for Qwen3, so it is unclear whether the contrastive objective—rather than simply any in-distribution fine-tuning—is responsible for the proof-setting gains. This weakens the claim that DAIL is the first to improve long-CoT reasoning directly from expert solutions.

The main contrastive loss equation in the provided manuscript appears garbled/incomplete: the negative-reference term and gamma are not visible in the displayed objective, making the central training objective hard to verify from the main text alone. The appendix ablation partly compensates, but the main equation should be complete and precise.

Reproducibility is incomplete. No code release, generated data release, or working URL for the promised el-proof dataset is provided. There are no random seeds, error bars, or variance estimates for the pass@k results, despite small evaluation sets (e.g., 60 AIME problems) and likely stochastic training/generation.

Potential benchmark contamination is only partially addressed. IMO-AnswerBench overlap with el-verifiable is checked post hoc, but the proof-setting deduplication and possible overlap with AIME 2024/2025 or BeyondAIME are not fully analyzed in the main paper. The appendix deduplication discussion for el-proof also confusingly refers to a 'final evaluation set' rather than the training set.

The negative-reference construction is heuristic and brittle: it extracts numeric/symbolic waypoints via regular expressions, which may be especially unreliable for proof problems. There is no sensitivity analysis to waypoint extraction quality and no quantitative measure of rationalization shortcuts or solution-citation artifacts in generated traces; the mixed-policy benefit is largely described qualitatively.

There is no explicit Limitations section. The paper does not sufficiently discuss failure cases, prompt sensitivity, dependence on a sufficiently competent student model, compute costs for dataset generation, or the limitations of applying the method outside mathematics.

Some generalization claims are slightly overstated. On GPQA-Diamond, Qwen2.5 DAIL pass@128 is actually lower than base (84.3 vs 85.9), so 'matches or outperforms across most settings' should be stated more carefully.

The RLVR comparisons are informative but not fully apples-to-apples: DAIL uses expert solutions while GRPO/NuRL use only reward signals, so the comparison illustrates the motivation rather than isolating method quality under equal information.

strengths: Targets an important and real failure mode of RLVR: hard problems often yield zero reward, and non-verifiable expert data cannot be used by standard RL. DAIL offers a practical offline way to learn from fewer than 1000 expert solutions.

The two-stage design is well motivated: expert-conditioned self-distillation bridges the distribution gap between didactic human solutions and the model's own reasoning, while the negative-reference contrastive loss is a sensible mechanism to avoid learning rationalization shortcuts.

The empirical evaluation is broad: AIME 2024/2025, BeyondAIME, IMO-AnswerBench, GPQA-Diamond, plus Maze, Rotten Oranges, HealthBench, and Tool Alpaca in the appendix, across Qwen2.5-Instruct and Qwen3-8B/14B.
Baselines are strong and include direct SFT on expert solutions, STaR rationalization, GRPO, NuRL+GRPO, GRPO on >40K DeepScaleR examples, temperature variation, and distillation from Qwen3-235B-A22B.
Ablations isolate the main components: contrastive vs NLL, mixed policy vs direct sampling, negative-reference loss variants, token budget, model scale, and standard distillation.

Efficiency claims are well supported: offline generation is decoupled from training, LoRA adapters share a single frozen base model, post-generation training is reported at 0.1 H100 hours/epoch, and token-budget results show roughly 2x token reduction for comparable coverage.
The paper is generally honest about limitations: weaker models such as Llama-3.1-8B do not improve, pass@1 sometimes drops, and deduplication/leakage checks are reported.
No material ethical concerns are apparent: expert data sourcing is described, the el-proof dataset is released, and the impact statement discusses potential safety-related applications.
weaknesses: The contrastive objective is not fully specified in the main text; the displayed equation is incomplete and the sign/placement of gamma and the negative term must be inferred from later ablation text. This limits reproducibility and theoretical clarity.

For LRMs, rollouts are truncated at 256 tokens, but the paper does not clearly explain how these truncated traces are used for training or how they teach full long-CoT reasoning. This is a significant reproducibility and soundness gap.

The central non-verifiable proof setting is not evaluated on proof generation or proof quality; all main evaluations are answer-verifiable math/science benchmarks. The claim that DAIL enables learning from non-verifiable proofs is therefore only indirectly supported.

pass@1 frequently decreases relative to the base model (e.g., AIME 8.8 vs 9.8, IMO 6.4 vs 6.8), and the paper does not fully resolve this practical tradeoff. Some abstract claims such as 'up to 31%' and 'double reasoning efficiency' are not straightforwardly derived from the main tables.
pass@k results lack confidence intervals or significance tests. With 60-400 evaluation problems, several reported gains may be within noise, and gamma is tuned on a small 100-sample validation set.

For Qwen3 on el-proof, the baseline comparison is thin: there is no SFT/STaR on expert proofs, and standard distillation from Qwen3-235B-A22B is better at higher token budgets (55 vs 49 at 4096), weakening claims of superiority.
The negative reference relies on regex-extracted intermediate results/waypoints. This is brittle and domain-specific, with no analysis of extraction quality, failure modes, or extension beyond math.

Several claims are overbroad (e.g., 'first demonstration') despite concurrent self-distillation work, and some non-math/OOD results are only appendix-level with mixed outcomes, such as HealthBench total score being essentially flat.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and well-motivated problem: extracting training signal from high-quality expert solutions on problems where RLVR stalls because the model cannot sample a correct rollout (zero-advantage regime).

The two-stage DAIL recipe (in-distribution expansion via mixed policy rollouts + contrastive learning to suppress shortcut imitation) is a reasonable and reasonably novel combination, and the mixed-policy decoding idea (student proposes, teacher verifies against a threshold) is a sensible mechanism.

The empirical study is broad: multiple benchmarks (AIME 2024/25, BeyondAIME, IMO-AnswerBench, GPQA), multiple backbones (Qwen2.5-Instruct, Qwen3-8B/14B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama, Llama-3.1-8B), and non-math domains (Maze, Rotten Oranges, HealthBench, Tool Alpaca).

The ablation in Table 9 directly supports the design of the contrastive objective: the contrastive loss (46.0) outperforms teacher-only KL (44.0), and minimizing divergence to the negative reference degrades performance (38.1), matching the stated motivation.

Efficiency is quantified concretely (token-budget coverage in Figure 4 and training-compute comparison in Appendix C.6), and the offline formulation's efficiency advantage over online RLVR is a legitimate practical benefit.
The paper is candid about failure modes: it reports that weaker models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-4B, R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) show little or no improvement, and it acknowledges the pass@1/pass@k tradeoff.
weaknesses: The central contribution—the contrastive objective—is not fully specified. The displayed loss equation is truncated and shows only the positive teacher-KL term; the full objective incorporating the negative-reference term and the hyperparameter γ is never written out. The text only says γ controls the effect of the negative reference. This is a critical reproducibility/soundness gap for the paper's main novelty, unless it is purely a PDF-rendering artifact (the authors should ensure the complete formula is present).

A standard distillation baseline from a much larger model (Qwen3-235B-A22B) matches or beats DAIL at higher token budgets (Table 10: 24 vs 23 at 1024, 37 vs 34 at 2048, 55 vs 49 at 4096). This substantially weakens the claim that DAIL is an 'attractive' alternative, and undercuts the headline significance framing.

The out-of-domain generalization claim is weakly supported. In Table 1, Qwen2.5 pass@128 is 84.3 (DAIL) vs 85.9 (base)—DAIL is worse—and most other differences are within sampling noise. The summary 'matches or outperforms' overstates a result that is largely 'no significant change.'

No variance, confidence intervals, or seed information is reported for the main pass@k results. With n=128 samples per problem, many reported differences (e.g., GPQA pass@1 34.1 vs 35.1; AIME pass@1 9.8 vs 8.8) are plausibly within noise, so the strength of several claims cannot be assessed.

The negative-reference construction is a crude heuristic: it extracts numbers/waypoints via a handful of regular expressions and conditions on them to induce 'rationalization shortcuts.' The premise that this specific context reliably induces shortcut-laden reasoning—and that the induced distribution is the right negative signal—is asserted rather than validated.

The RLVR comparison is partly a strawman: GRPO on the 417 problems that the base model failed 32 times is expected to fail (near-zero reward), so its degradation is unsurprising and does not establish DAIL's superiority over RLVR in general. The comparison to a realistic large RLVR run (DeepScaleR) is more informative but shows only marginal differences.

The abstract claims 'up to 31% pass@128 gains,' but the largest gains visible in the reported tables/figures are roughly 13–22% relative (e.g., IMO-AnswerBench 33.5→37.8; AIME 51.7→63.3). The provenance of the 31% figure is not clearly traceable from the presented results.
Provenance of the newly released el-proof dataset is vague ('sourced ... from website with permission'), which is insufficient for a resource the paper advertises as a public contribution.

The mixed-policy threshold τ=0.8 is calibrated on training-set performance (Appendix C.3), which risks overfitting the generation hyperparameter; the description of the rollout mechanism is also somewhat ambiguous.

The reported efficiency gains are attributed qualitatively ('high information density ... inherent in expert traces') without direct measurement of redundancy or circular reasoning, leaving the mechanism for the 2× token efficiency claim unverified.

strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in RLVR: on extremely difficult problems, reward/advantage is often zero, so expert human solutions provide an alternative learning signal. DAIL is a plausible and well-motivated response.

The two-stage method is novel and technically interesting: mixed policy rollouts convert out-of-distribution expert solutions into in-distribution traces, and a contrastive objective is used to penalize rationalization shortcuts.

Empirical scope is broad: two model families (Qwen2.5-Instruct, Qwen3-8B/14B), two training datasets (417 verifiable AIME problems, 669 Olympiad proof problems), several benchmarks (AIME 2024/25, BeyondAIME, IMO-AnswerBench, GPQA-Diamond), and multiple baselines (SFT, STaR, GRPO, NuRL+GRPO, DeepScaleR GRPO).

Main pass@k results are promising and consistent across benchmarks: e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct improves from 51.7 to 63.3 on AIME pass@128, 41.0 to 46.0 on BeyondAIME pass@128, and 33.5 to 37.8 on IMO-AnswerBench pass@128, while RLVR baselines often degrade at large k.

The ablation analysis is useful: NLL vs. contrastive loss, direct sampling vs. mixed policy rollouts, and training-vs-test performance to argue that NLL/RLVR learn shortcuts while DAIL generalizes better.

Practical efficiency is well argued: offline data generation decouples rollouts from optimization, and LoRA plus adapter toggling allows teacher and negative-reference forward passes without storing multiple model copies. The claimed 0.1 H100 hours/epoch vs. 277.6 for GRPO is a compelling efficiency advantage if accurate.
The paper provides detailed prompts, hyperparameters, and dataset construction details, and releases the el-proof dataset as a new resource.
The limitations section and appendices discuss weaker models, other domains, and on-policy variants, showing some awareness of scope and failure modes.
weaknesses: The central contrastive loss equation appears incomplete/truncated in the manuscript: the displayed formula only shows the KL term to the teacher and omits the negative-reference term and how gamma enters, making the exact objective hard to reproduce.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple training seeds are reported for the main results. Many headline gains are on small benchmarks (e.g., BeyondAIME has 100 problems), so differences such as 46.0 vs. 44.0 for the contrastive ablation could be within run-to-run noise.

The non-verifiable proof setting is not directly evaluated: the model is trained on Olympiad proofs but evaluated only on answer-verifiable benchmarks. There is no proof-generation or proof-correctness evaluation, so the claim about learning from non-verifiable proof problems is only partially supported.

For Qwen3 reasoning models, mixed-policy rollouts are truncated at 256 tokens. This is very short for long-CoT and proof reasoning; the paper does not show the length or quality of the resulting el-proof traces, nor does it justify how 256-token traces teach long-CoT reasoning.

The negative reference is constructed with heuristic regular expressions that extract numerical/symbolic waypoints. There is no validation that this actually induces rationalization shortcuts, and the contrastive objective's benefit over positive-only KL is modest (46.0 vs. 44.0 on BeyondAIME).

The comparison to distillation from Qwen3-235B-A22B shows the stronger teacher outperforms DAIL at higher token budgets (55 vs. 49 at 4096 tokens). DAIL is therefore mainly useful when no stronger teacher exists, which limits the strength of the 'similar coverage' claim.

Pass@1 can degrade relative to the base model: on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, DAIL lowers IMO-AnswerBench pass@1 from 6.8 to 6.4 and AIME pass@1 from 9.8 to 8.8. Qwen3 pass@1 gains are marginal and become negative at 4096 tokens, so practical utility depends on large-k sampling.

Hyperparameter tuning is somewhat fragile: tau is calibrated on the training set, and gamma is tuned on only 100 validation examples. This raises concerns about overfitting and whether the same hyperparameters transfer across models and datasets.

Reproducibility and ethics are incompletely addressed: no code release is mentioned, and copyright/licensing of AoPS community solutions and the sourced IMO proof data is not discussed. The abstract's 'up to 31% pass@128 gains' is not clearly traceable to the reported tables for Qwen2.5 (gains are roughly 12-22%).

There are presentation issues: inconsistent naming ('el-verifiable' vs. 'e1-verifiable'), an incomplete central equation, and some ambiguous figure descriptions. These make the method harder to follow and reproduce than it should be.
